reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The .359 xwOBA and 49.0% hard-hit rate sit in the top tier of contact quality, but a 27.0% strikeout rate and 34.1% chase rate are the friction points keeping the floor honest. The xBA landing at .251 is what that looks like in practice: power that translates, average that doesn't fully follow. What makes the profile work anyway is the 11.9% walk rate pulling the OBP toward .367 in the projection, and 29.5 ft/s sprint speed that turns baserunning into a separate weapon, projecting to 38 stolen bases alongside 37 home runs. If he ever tightens the zone discipline enough to shave the chase rate, the xwOBA already says the power is pointed at something big; if he doesn't, this is still a very useful player, just one who runs a high-variance at-bat until further notice.

reports.name: Bobby Witt Jr.
reports.published_report: The .379 xwOBA and .500 xSLG are doing exactly what you'd expect from a 92.3 mph average exit velocity paired with 51.0% hard contact, and the projection's .285/.358/.464 line is the conservative translation of a Statcast profile that reads 98th percentile in expected batting average. The one real friction in this profile is a 33.3% chase rate that sits well below average, a vulnerability pitchers will keep testing; so far the 17.5% strikeout rate says he's managing it, but that's the hinge. Add 30.1 ft/s sprint speed at the 99th percentile and the 41 projected steals aren't a rounding error, they're load-bearing. He's a perennial top-tier fantasy shortstop until the chase rate stops being manageable, and there's no current evidence it's becoming that.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: The Statcast batting profile sits at .409 xwOBA and .580 xSLG, two figures that describe a hitter most pitchers face maybe twice a year. What makes it credible isn't just the raw violence, 93.5 mph average exit velocity and a 16.7% barrel rate, but the 13.1% walk rate sitting alongside it, a pairing that says he earns his damage rather than stumbling into it. The pitching side is almost equally absurd: a 2.72 xERA and 30.4% whiff rate from an arm running 98.1 mph with 2488 rpm of spin, and a 3.8% barrel rate allowed that tells you hitters aren't squaring him up even when they make contact. The whole profile hinges on his body holding a workload that no one in the sport has sustained long-term, and if the elbow or the shoulder forces a choice, you lose whichever half gets shelved. Assuming he stays whole, the projection of .287/.387/.555 with 39 home runs across 690 plate appearances is less a ceiling than a reasonable median for someone whose Statcast profile in both directions looks like two different All-Stars sharing one roster spot.

Misiorowski's 38.1% whiff rate and 2632 rpm on the fastball explain the swing-and-miss volume, and a 3.2% barrel rate tells you the contact that does happen isn't doing damage. reports.name: Jordan Walker
reports.published_report: The contact-quality profile and the swing decisions point in opposite directions, and that gap is the whole Walker argument. His 92.6 mph average exit velocity sits in the 94th percentile, barrel rate is 13.4%, and his .356 xwOBA says the damage when he connects is genuine, full-count talent. The problem is a 35.8% chase rate and 30.4% whiff rate that bleed strikeouts and shrink his walk total, keeping the plate discipline closer to liability than asset. If he tightens the zone even modestly, the projection's .282/.342/.489 with 30 home runs and 21 stolen bases is what you get, one of the more complete offensive profiles in the league. If the chase rate stays where it is, you're backing a boom-or-bust hitter carrying a real contact risk, which caps the floor somewhere around a second-division regular who punishes mistakes but gets eaten by quality stuff.

reports.name: Sal Stewart
reports.published_report: The xSLG and xwOBA tell the same story: a 13.4% barrel rate doing serious work on contact quality that a middling hard-hit rate undersells. Stewart doesn't beat you with raw exit velocity across the board, he beats you in barrels specifically, and that's why the .473 xSLG lands where it does while the 38.4% hard-hit rate sits below the median. The 27.1% whiff rate is the thing to watch — if pitchers find a consistent exploitable zone, the in-zone contact quality that drives the .348 xwOBA gets tested, and you're left with a corner bat whose average stays closer to .253 than anything prettier. Hold that, and a 33-homer, 15-steal season at 692 projected plate appearances is a reasonable outcome for a 22-year-old.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: Thirty-five home runs and 30 steals from a shortstop is a rare combination, and the Statcast profile explains how it's happening without being a pure contact story. The power reads as legitimate at a 10.3% barrel rate with an .xSLG of .446, even though the 89.5 mph average exit velocity is right at the median, because he's generating barrels efficiently rather than just mashing everything hard. What makes him genuinely dangerous is that the projection's .273/.347/.511 line assumes his legs keep doing real work alongside the pop, and at 28.5 ft/s he has the speed to post 30 steals in a full season. The catch in the profile is the 37.2% chase rate, which is a real liability, and if pitchers learn to exploit it more aggressively the strikeouts climb past 23.2% and the walks stay stuck near 8.6%, which puts pressure on everything downstream.

reports.name: James Wood

The one live wire in the profile is a 28.6% strikeout rate, and the bet Wood is making, successfully so far, is that a 16.8% walk rate keeps enough plate appearances from ending in outs that the strikeouts don't drain what the power produces. If pitchers ever find a consistent way to exploit that 30.7% whiff rate, the walk rate is what keeps him from sliding into a boom-or-bust corner type; if they don't, the projection's .388 OBP and 35 home runs are a floor, not a ceiling.

Carroll's 91.6 mph average exit velocity and 48.1% hard-hit rate are the kind of contact quality numbers that support real power, and the .344 xwOBA backs that up — the gap between that and his actual production is where the projection lives. The 11.9% barrel rate and 11.9% walk rate together describe a patient, impactful hitter; the walk rate sits well above average, which is what keeps the .346 OBP credible even when the .247 xBA signals his batting average ceiling is modest. At 29.7 ft/s sprint speed he's in elite company on the bases, and the projection's 23 steals across 683 PA undersells what that speed does to a defense when paired with a .346 OBP. The one dependency: that 27.2% whiff rate is the thing keeping his floor lower than his tools, and if the contact quality is there but the contact rate doesn't improve, the home run totals come in lumpy rather than consistently.

reports.name: Eli Willits
reports.published_report: Eighty-eight walks at 18 years old, against 92 strikeouts, across 463 plate appearances split between A and A+: the discipline is the entire argument. That translates to a 13.2% walk rate in MLB context, roughly where the upper tier of patient hitters lives, which means the zone command is already a carrying tool and not a future hope. The power across A+ & A sits at .198 ISO with 13 home runs, but the MLB-equivalent translation comes out at .134, short of where impact bats tend to land, so the ceiling as an everyday shortstop depends on whether that gap closes as he fills out physically. If it doesn't, what remains is a high-OBP table-setter with 53 stolen bases, a profile that fits a regular better than a bench role, but only just.

reports.name: Kade Anderson
reports.published_report: A 1.1 ERA and a 0.6 WHIP at Double-A aren't numbers that need context — they're the argument. Anderson has struck out 135 batters against 13 walks across 93.3 innings at AA this season, and the command profile translates cleanly: a BB/9 of 2.0 in MLB terms, well below the 3.2 figure where most pitchers land, with a K-BB% that comes out to 21.9% against an average of 13.5%. The whole thing hinges on whether the stuff backs up the control at the highest level, because a left-hander this young who misses this many bats while almost never missing the zone has no obvious developmental ceiling short of a frontline starter. If the stuff softens in the jump, he's still a useful mid-rotation arm, but nothing in this line suggests you should expect softening.

Contact quality is genuinely there: an xwOBA of .350 and xBA of .275 say his bat-to-ball results, when he does connect, play at an above-average level, and 28.8 ft/s sprint speed keeps the stolen base threat real at 21 projected bags. reports.name: Jac Caglianone
reports.published_report: The contact quality is elite and the discipline is not. Caglianone's 93.2 mph average exit velocity and 55.0% hard-hit rate sit at the very top of the league, and the .514 xSLG says the power translates — 28 home runs in the projection is a floor, not a ceiling, if he can keep the barrel on balls he swings at. The problem is a 38.4% chase rate and a 6.3% walk rate that together describe a hitter who will hand pitchers an easy route: throw him breaking stuff down and away, let him expand, and bypass the damage entirely. If the zone-recognition improves even modestly, this is a middle-of-the-order bat; if it doesn't, the .276/.330/.491 projection line is roughly what he is, a punishing contact maker who leaves too many free outs on the table.

reports.name: Otto Lopez

The power is modest, barrel rate at 6.2%, which keeps the projection's .44 SLG honest, and the OPS projection of .780 is essentially what you get when a plus contact profile runs into a below-average walk rate. What carries the profile beyond solid-regular territory is the sprint speed at 28.5 ft/s, with 29 projected steals a meaningful real-world contribution, and the 97th-percentile OAA grade puts him among the best defenders at his positions. He's an everyday middle infielder whose ceiling is capped by the fact that he won't draw the walks to get into hitter's counts more often, and if that chase rate creeps up, the .302 AVG that holds the projection together starts to erode.

report_llm.text: The xBA sits at .283 — 92nd percentile — on an exit velocity of 86.3 mph, which tells you almost everything about the profile: he's winning with contact quality, bat-to-ball, and a 28.8 ft/s sprint speed, not by hitting the ball hard. The projected .302 AVG over 623 PA is believable precisely because of that xBA shape, even with a 2.7% barrel rate that ranks near the bottom of the league. This whole profile hinges on whether he stays in the lineup; the OBP at .359 looks generous relative to a 6.7% walk rate, and if the batting average regresses toward his actual contact outcomes rather than above them, the offensive case thins quickly. What you get if it clicks is a high-average second baseman who runs well and plays multiple spots; what's left if the average fades is a below-average bat with no power to carry it.

reports.name: Héctor Rodríguez
reports.published_report: The .259 ISO at AAA is loud for a 22-year-old, and the translation says it carries: an MLB-equivalent ISO of .190 against a big-league context where .150 is the baseline. The discipline profile is the honest constraint — 42 walks against 93 strikeouts in 455 AAA plate appearances translates to a walk rate and a strikeout rate that both land right at MLB average, which means the bat has to carry him with no margin for a power regression. If the raw over-the-fence ability holds at the big-league level, Héctor Rodríguez is a real bench bat who can be deployed against righties; if the power thins out in translation, the walk rate won't save the profile.

reports.name: Cam Caminiti
reports.published_report: The 3.70 ERA across AA & A+ looks good; what's underneath it is more complicated. Caminiti's 106 strikeouts in 97.6 innings translate to a 7.8 K/9 at the MLB level, a tick below what MLB starters average, and his 45 walks push his translated BB/9 to 4.3 against an MLB mean of 3.2. The 1.20 WHIP with an 85th-percentile mark in his pitcher pool suggests he's managing contact well enough to keep the walks from fully cashing, which is the load-bearing beam in this profile right now. If the command develops and the walk rate comes down, he's a back-end starter; if it doesn't, you're left with a depth arm who lives on contact suppression longer than he should have to.

reports.name: Caleb Durbin
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is almost entirely a contact-and-speed story, because the power isn't there. An 83.8 mph average exit velocity and a 26.1% hard-hit rate sit at the very bottom of the league, and the .326 xSLG bears that out — so the projection's 15 home runs hinge entirely on volume, on Durbin getting to 590 plate appearances and squeezing every cheap one out. What keeps him interesting is the 13.5% strikeout rate, which is genuinely elite, and 21 projected steals give him a path to value that doesn't require him to punish the ball. If the contact quality stays this soft, he's a useful table-setter with a real defensive asset at third, but the ceiling is a second-division regular who needs a lot of things to go right to reach it.

reports.name: Cam Smith
reports.published_report: The 11.8% barrel rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, and it's the right kind of work. Smith's .440 xSLG suggests legitimate over-the-fence pop, the 45.2% hard-hit rate backs the shape, and at 29.3 ft/s he's a genuine weapon on the bases when he gets on — the problem is getting on, because a 29.0% whiff rate against a 7.7% walk rate leaves the .294 OBP looking like a ceiling, not a floor. The projection's .225 AVG with 21 home runs across a full season sketches the profile clearly: a second-division regular with a real power tool and an on-base limitation that keeps the overall value modest. If the whiff rate comes down even a little, the .440 xSLG has room to fully materialize; if it doesn't, the gap between what he does to the balls he hits and what he does against the actual strike zone stays the story.

reports.name: Dillon Dingler
reports.published_report: Thirty-one projected home runs from a catcher who doesn't even rank in the top third of the league in average exit velocity is the whole puzzle with Dingler. The .488 xSLG and .358 xwOBA say he's getting to his power through contact quality and barrel rate, not raw thump, which is a profile that holds as long as his 33.6% chase rate doesn't creep upward and turn his 6.2% walk rate into a real liability. If the plate discipline stays where it is, the projection to .795 OPS across a full season is a legitimate everyday catcher profile, maybe the most valuable position-adjusted bat in Detroit's lineup. The walk rate is thin enough that any regression in pitch recognition shrinks this from an offensive asset to a solid-but-ordinary backstop fast.

reports.name: MacKenzie Gore
reports.published_report: The contact suppression doesn't match the strikeout rate, and that gap is the whole profile. Gore misses bats at a 25.8% clip, but a 42.0% hard-hit rate and an 8.8% barrel rate tell you hitters who make contact are doing damage, which is why the xERA sits at 3.87 while the projection lands at 4.29. The walk rate at 8.5% is the real pressure point: he can live with the contact quality if he's pitching ahead, and the 196 projected strikeouts across 176.8 innings suggest he's getting enough swings and misses to survive it, but the margin for error tightens whenever the command drifts. If the walk rate tightens, he's a legitimate mid-rotation arm; if it stays where it is, 4.29 is probably the floor, not the ceiling.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The gap between a 3.55 ERA projection and a 4.20 xERA is the whole tension in this profile. Weathers misses bats at a 25.4% strikeout rate with a 6.9% walk rate, both sitting comfortably above average, but his 29.2% chase rate is below average and his contact quality numbers are soft — 41.1% hard-hit, 8.4% barrels, 89.4 mph average exit velocity all clustering in the bottom third of the league. The read on him is a pitcher who generates whiffs in the zone rather than coaxing chases, which works until it doesn't, because hitters who don't expand will eventually get to 95.8 mph heat when their counts are favorable. If the strikeout and walk rates hold at their current shape across 167.2 projected innings, he's a back-end starter worth rostering; if the contact suppression regresses toward what his xERA already suggests, the ERA follows it up.

reports.name: Justin Crawford

The .257 xBA gives him a real batting average floor, but the .320 xSLG explains why the projection lands at .682 OPS across 476 PA, because there's essentially no power to carry him when the hit rate dips. reports.name: Cole Carrigg
reports.published_report: At 28.8 ft/s, Carrigg sits at the 87th percentile in sprint speed, and 14 projected stolen bases might actually undersell what those legs can do over a full season. The .347 OBP running above his .272 average suggests he's earning his way on base rather than just barreling everything, which matters in a Colorado lineup that opposing pitchers can attack without much fear. The projection is for 373 plate appearances, so the Rockies haven't committed to him full-time yet, and that's the real hinge: if the contact and on-base skills hold against a full rotation of major-league arms, he profiles as a second-division regular with speed adding value everywhere. If the bat thins out, the 76th-percentile fielding and those wheels keep him as a useful fourth outfielder rather than a sunk cost.

His 17.2% barrel rate and 92.8 mph average exit velocity sit at the very top of the league, and his 14.7% walk rate means pitchers who work around him pay for it. The catch is the 33.8% strikeout rate, which drags his xBA down to .236 and is why a .876 OPS hitter carries a .240 average, but the power and patience are genuine enough that the strikeouts are a known cost, not a correctable flaw. At 33, he is what he is: a DH-profile masher who gets on base, hits the ball over the fence at an elite rate, and costs you a quarter of his at-bats to do it.

reports.name: Seaver King
reports.published_report: The .319/.401/.545 line across AAA & AA is loud, and the translation brings it back to earth just enough to matter. At MLB rates, the ISO softens to .167 and the strikeout rate climbs to 22.8% — roughly league average on both counts, not a problem, just a different player than the minor-league numbers suggest. The walk rate translates cleanly at 8.9%, and 12 stolen bases in 385 PA hints at a profile with enough speed to add value in ways the slash line doesn't capture. The whole thing hinges on whether the .376 BABIP has enough contact quality behind it to survive a major-league defense, because if that number regresses hard, the ISO translation is already thin enough that the bat becomes a bench piece rather than a regular.

reports.name: Jakob Marsee
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries this profile. At 12.8% he's drawing free passes at a rate most hitters in his class can't match, and a 22.8% chase rate explains why — he rarely goes fishing, which is how a guy with a 3.6% barrel rate and 87.1 mph average exit velocity still posts a .323 OBP in the projection. The contact quality is genuinely thin, xBA sitting at .220 and xSLG at .314, so this whole thing hinges on whether the plate discipline keeps translating to on-base value or pitchers learn to attack him in the zone and expose the lack of impact. If the zone command holds, he's a useful fourth outfielder who runs (25 projected steals) and gets on base despite not hurting anyone; if it cracks, the .209 projected average has nowhere to hide.

reports.name: Karson Milbrandt
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate translates, the walk rate doesn't. Across AAA & AA this season, Milbrandt has struck out 110 batters in 89.3 innings, and the K/9 of 11.1 converts to a solid 9.1 at the MLB level. But 53 walks in that same sample pushes his translated BB/9 to 4.8, and the gap between his raw strikeout punch and his control is what keeps a K-BB% of 16 in the minors from meaning much in the bigs. If the zone command sharpens, he's a multi-inning or setup arm with a real weapon; if it doesn't, he's depth.

reports.name: Travis Bazzana
reports.published_report: The walk rate carries the argument here. Bazzana's 11.6% BB rate is a legitimate separator, and his chase rate of 25.9% confirms he's genuinely difficult to expand against, but the contact quality tells a different story entirely, with an xBA of .223 and an xSLG of .349 sitting in the bottom sixth of the league. The projection (.234/.328/.372 across 520 PA) reflects exactly that split: a hitter who earns first base at a useful clip but doesn't do enough damage when he makes contact to carry a lineup spot. He's a second-division regular if the plate discipline holds and the exit velocity develops beyond 88.1 mph; if the contact quality doesn't improve, the profile thins to a high-OBP bench piece who can run a little.

reports.name: Emerson Hancock
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the only reason to believe in the projection. Hancock's Statcast profile is nearly undifferentiated at the percentile level, xERA at 3.98, K% at 23.1, whiff rate and chase rate both in the bottom third, but a 6.2% BB% puts him in the 85th percentile for command, and that's doing real load-bearing work when nothing else stands out. The 3.52 ERA projection over 164.4 innings is essentially a bet that plus control and a 95.4 mph fastball are enough to keep a mediocre contact profile from fully cashing out, even when hitters are barreling him at 8.4% and posting a 41.1% hard-hit rate. If the command holds, he's a back-end starter who earns his innings; if the contact suppression doesn't improve, the walk rate alone can't carry a rotation job and he becomes a long relief option with a serviceable ceiling.

reports.name: Caden Bodine
reports.published_report: Twenty-six strikeouts in 468 plate appearances across A, A+, and AA. That's not a misprint, and the 6 K% translates to an 11.4% rate in MLB context, well below where most big-league hitters land. The contact is the whole argument here, and it's a loud one: the .412 OBP sits at the 94th percentile in his hitter pool, built almost entirely on the bat making contact rather than the walk rate, which translates to just 8.2% at the MLB level. The ceiling question isn't whether he can reach the big leagues; it's whether a catcher with fringy raw power, an MLB-equivalent ISO of .121 where the league average sits at .150, can do enough damage to hold a lineup spot, and if the bat slips even a little at the highest level, what's left is a bench piece worth carrying for the glove and the average.

reports.name: Coby Mayo
reports.published_report: The contact profile is genuinely alarming: a 31.9% whiff rate sitting at the 10th percentile, a 32.6% strikeout rate at the 3rd, and an xBA of .220 that reflects not bad luck but a real inability to put the barrel on the ball consistently. What saves the conversation is that the contact he does make is legitimately hard, a 92.3 mph average exit velocity at the 91st percentile and a 49.0% hard-hit rate, which is why the xSLG sits at .431 and the projected 21 home runs over 426 plate appearances aren't a fantasy. The entire profile hinges on whether he can close the gap between how hard he hits it and how often he misses it entirely, because right now those two things are pulling in violently different directions. If the whiff rate comes down even modestly, there's a fringe-regular first baseman here; if it doesn't, .216 with 21 home runs is a roster decision waiting to happen.

reports.name: Jacob Latz
reports.published_report: The xERA and xwOBA are both sitting at the 98th percentile, and that's the whole argument for Latz. His 35.5% chase rate explains why contact is so suppressed: hitters are expanding, and when they do make contact, the barrel rate is just 5.3%. The walk rate at 7.3% is ordinary, not a weapon, so the profile hinges on that chase number staying where it is, because the fastball at 94.7 mph isn't overpowering anyone who sits back and waits. If the chase dries up, you've got a middle reliever with average velocity and nothing scary behind it; if it holds, the projection of 30 saves in 70.3 innings at a 2.13 ERA starts to look like an accurate description of a genuine late-inning closer.

reports.name: Xavier Isaac
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the lead. At AA in 412 plate appearances, Isaac has drawn 78 walks against 116 strikeouts, and the translation puts that at a 14% BB rate where the MLB average sits at 8.5% — a real edge that doesn't need the rest of the profile to work. The rest does work: .254 ISO at AA and 23 home runs paired with 18 stolen bases sketch a hitter with genuine pull-side pop and enough athleticism to punish mistakes in multiple directions. The problem is the strikeout shape, because 28% at AA translates to 29% against major-league pitching, and for a first baseman with no defensive flexibility, the power and patience have to carry that weight entirely. If the strikeouts compress and the .405 OBP shape holds, there's an everyday regular in this profile; if they don't, he lands as a platoon bat whose on-base skills keep him useful without ever becoming indispensable.

reports.name: Jackson Kent
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing a lot of work here, and it's holding up. Across AAA & AA this season, 30 walks in 94.4 innings translates to a BB/9 of 3.1 at the MLB equivalent, virtually identical to the 3.2 pitchers run on average, and the WHIP of 1.1 is the spine of a 3.7 ERA that grades out cleanly against the competition. The K-BB% of 20% across those levels translates to 14.5% in MLB terms, a tick above the league mean, which means the profile isn't built on strikeouts he doesn't quite own, his 10.0 K/9 in the minors comes back to 8.6 in translation, it's built on not giving hitters free passes. If the command holds in full-time big-league exposure, he's a multi-inning reliever with a real job; if it slips, 105 strikeouts don't leave enough margin to survive, and you're looking at a depth arm filling innings when someone goes down.

reports.name: Adrian Santana
reports.published_report: The contact is the carrying tool, and everything else is the question. Across AA & A+, Santana is hitting .302 with just 31 strikeouts in 291 plate appearances, an 11% rate that translates to roughly 16.7% against big-league pitching, comfortably rarer than what most MLB lineups produce. The problem is that the ISO sitting at .081 across those same levels translates to .094 at the MLB equivalent, about sixty points shy of the MLB average of .15, and the 3 home runs confirm this is a bat that has to manufacture everything it creates, hence the 23 stolen bases doing real work in the OPS. reports.name: Fenwick Trimble
reports.published_report: The speed-power combination is louder than the ceiling. Eighteen stolen bases and 14 home runs across 350 AA plate appearances is a real offensive toolkit, and the .199 ISO confirms the pop isn't just a counting-number trick at a hitter-friendly level. The translation is where it gets honest: that ISO dials down to .151 at the MLB level, landing right at league average, and the walk rate translates to 7.9% against a league that runs at 8.5%, meaning the on-base profile doesn't carry the slugging when the power compresses. If the speed ages well and the hit tool (.263/.340 in AA) holds its shape, he's a useful fourth outfielder who runs into value; if the contact doesn't sharpen at Triple-A, you're looking at an organizational depth piece in the Marlins' system.
